And I genuinely don't understand why.

My name is Bec I'm 31 years old.

And for two years, I've been trying to figure out why my daughter won't potty train.

Not "won't try."

Won't train.

She's smart. She can read some words. She knows her numbers. 

She follows instructions perfectly.

But potty training? Nothing sticks.

And the confusing part is her younger brother trained at 2 and a half.

No issues. No drama. He just got it.

So what's different?

data.caption: gonest.homes
data.copy:
Both pans in this photograph were sold with the same word on the box: titanium.

One of them is titanium. The other is the reason a home cook named Marta spent 2 years believing titanium was a scam.

The black pan on the left was sold at a titanium price, the kind of price you accept because you believe you're buying a metal that lasts forever. The listing used the word "titanium" 11 times, titanium-reinforced, titanium-strengthened, Titanium Pro. She read that the way anyone would: she was buying a titanium pan. That is exactly what she was meant to read.

14 months later, it looked the way it looks in this photo. Scratched through, flaking, sticking, shedding its surface into her food. And when she sat down, angry, to figure out how a titanium pan wears out, titanium doesn't wear out, that's the entire point of titanium, she found out what she had actually bought.

An aluminum pan. With a nonstick coating. The same PTFE-family coating that has been failing on pans since the sixties. The "titanium" was a sprinkle of titanium particles mixed into that coating, just enough to put the word on the box. The metal under her food was never titanium. Not one gram of the pan's body. She had paid for titanium and received aluminum wearing a costume.

Here is the part that made her genuinely angry: it isn't an exception. It's standard practice. Most pans sold as "titanium" are built exactly this way, aluminum bodies, wear-out coatings, titanium prices and the label words give it away. "Reinforced." "Infused." "Ceramic-titanium." "Titanium PLY." Every one of those words means the same thing: coating. Nobody regulates the word "titanium" on cookware. The word justifies the price, the coating fails on schedule, the customer buys again. That is the business model.

data.copy:
That white ring on your table?

It's not a stain. It's trapped moisture.

I stared at one on my dining table for eleven months before I learned that.

I thought the wood was permanently damaged. I thought my only options were sanding it down or living with it.

I tried toothpaste. Nothing.

I tried the iron-and-towel trick from YouTube. Made it cloudier.

I tried mayo. Left overnight. Woke up to a mayo stain AND a water ring.

Then a furniture restorer told me something that changed everything:

"That white mark isn't damage. It's moisture trapped inside the finish. Get the moisture out and the ring disappears."

The problem is most products can't get below the finish. They sit on top and do nothing.

Luxgrove's oil actually penetrates through the finish and into the grain.

It dissolves the trapped moisture. Then the wax seals the surface so it can't get back in.

I put it on the ring that had been haunting me for almost a year.

Five minutes. Buffed it off. Gone.

Not faded. Not blended. Gone.

The wood underneath was perfectly fine the entire time.

I just needed something that could actually reach it.

data.caption: Impossible to Cut Your Cat's Nails? Read this ☝️
data.copy:
I stopped trimming my cat’s nails — not because it was hard, but because it was breaking her heart (and mine).

I’m 64.

I’ve had cats my whole life.

My 14-year-old tortie, Marigold, has always been the sweetest, gentlest soul…

Until I touch her paws.

Then she turns into a completely different animal. She twists and thrashes like she’s fighting for her life. She screams so loudly it breaks my heart. And I’m not exaggerating when I say I tried everything.

I tried the burrito method. She kicked her way out in eight seconds.

I tried clipping her while she slept. She woke up the second the clippers got near her paw.

I tried the two-towel trick with a treat in my mouth. She bit me.

I tried having two people hold her. She destroyed both of us.

I tried calming sprays, calming treats, and pheromone diffusers. None of it worked.

Meanwhile her nails kept getting worse.

They don’t retract anymore. They hook into the blankets, the carpet, and my sleeves. When she makes biscuits on my chest, those claws go straight through my skin. A five-minute cuddle leaves me scratched up and hesitant to let her near my face.

So I finally called the vet.

$95 for a nail trim — plus they wanted to sedate her because she’s “uncooperative.”

The last time they sedated her, she couldn’t walk straight for 36 hours. She just lay there, glassy-eyed and not herself. I cried more than she did.

The vet is 40 minutes away. I can’t drive at night anymore. And the thought of putting her through sedation every 4 to 6 weeks for the rest of her life felt like a slow cruelty I couldn’t keep choosing.

So I stopped trying to trim her nails.

And I let her file them down herself instead.

Here are the 5 reasons I now recommend this to every senior cat owner I know.

1. No more costly vet trips and surprise bills 💵

A nail trim at my vet is $95. Add the sedation fee they tack on when she won’t cooperate, the 40-minute drive each way, and the cost of arranging a ride…

data.caption: The 2-Minute Whitening Trick That Works
data.copy:
I wasted $850 on whitening products that burned my gums.

And my teeth were still yellow.

Let me tell you exactly what I tried. Because if you're reading this, you've probably tried the same things.

Started with whitening toothpaste. The one everyone says to try first. Used it twice a day for two solid months. Followed the instructions perfectly. Morning and night. Every single day.

Nothing.

Not even a shade lighter. My teeth looked exactly the same. Complete waste of $13.

So I moved on to whitening strips from Shoppers Drug Mart. Figured if toothpaste doesn't work, strips must be stronger, right?

That's when things got bad.

First time I used them, they slipped. The gel touched my gums. Within 20 minutes, my gums were burning. Properly burning. Not a little uncomfortable. Actual pain.

I rinsed my mouth. Looked in the mirror. My gums were bright red. Raw. Like I'd burned them on something hot.

It hurt to eat for two days.

I looked it up afterwards. The peroxide that makes them work is the same thing burning your gums. The whitening and the pain are the exact same chemical reaction — you can't have one without the other.

But I didn't give up.

Next, I tried gel trays. You know, the kind you're supposed to mould to your teeth. $55 for the kit.

First time I used it, gel leaked everywhere. Got on my tongue. Got on the inside of my cheeks. Tasted absolutely vile. Made my whole mouth feel weird.

I used it three times. Gave it a proper go. Zero results. Not even the tiniest bit whiter.

Binned it.

Then I started seeing ads for charcoal powder. "Natural whitening." Everyone on Instagram was using it. All these before and after photos.

Used it for a week. Made a black mess of my bathroom sink every single time. My teeth didn't look any whiter. Just... black while I was using it.

Then I started reading the reviews properly. Not the paid Instagram posts. Real reviews from real people.

data.caption: Stop Greasing Your Eye Bags. Start Draining Them.
data.copy:
I'm going to tell you something I've never said out loud.
For three months, I rubbed Preparation H under my eyes every morning before work. Hemorrhoid cream. On my face. Because some actor on a podcast said it was "Hollywood's secret for eye bags."

I'm 46 years old. I run a commercial insurance brokerage. And I was standing in my bathroom at 5:45 AM, dabbing rectal cream under my eyes with my ring finger, praying that nobody would ever find out.

It worked. For about an hour. A mild tightening. The bags looked slightly less swollen. Then it wore off. And by lunch, my face looked exactly the same — heavy, dark, exhausted. Like it always does. Like it has for over a decade.

What I didn't know — what nobody told me — is that the hydrocortisone in hemorrhoid cream causes permanent thinning of periorbital skin with repeated use. The skin under your eyes is already the thinnest skin on your body. I was accelerating its structural collapse for one hour of temporary tightening.

I was making the problem worse. Every single morning.

But that's what desperation does. It makes you do things you'd never admit to. Because when you've tried everything else and nothing has worked, you'll try anything.

And I had tried everything.

Caffeine rollers. Retinol serums that dried my skin until it cracked. Vitamin C drops that stung and oxidized in the bottle. Hyaluronic acid creams that plumped the surface for two hours and left the bags identical the next morning. A $38 jar of beef tallow because some fitness influencer said it was "what our ancestors used." It sealed moisture into my already waterlogged under-eye area and made the bags look puffier than before. Expensive Vaseline with a campfire story.

data.caption: FIFO took a toll on me
data.copy:
I was on my seventh swing and ready to walk away from the best FIFO job I'd ever had because my feet were absolutely rooted.

$145K a year. Coming from $95K.

That extra $50,000 was everything. Two kids under ten. Wife working part-time around school hours. Finally ahead on bills instead of constantly scrambling.

But seven swings in, I was lying awake in my donga at 2am doing the math on chucking it in.

FMG site. Fourteen days on, seven days off. Twelve-hour shifts standing on concrete and crusher dust. Steel-cap boots mandatory.

The money was bloody incredible. The roster was solid. The crew was good.

But every single swing felt like my feet were getting absolutely hammered by lunchtime.

Started around my 3rd swing. Heels aching by smoko. By arvo crib, this sharp stabbing pain shooting up through my arches. By knock-off, I'd be hobbling back to my donga trying not to let the boys see.

This deep, grinding agony in my heels. Like bone scraping directly on concrete with every step. Burning sensation that made me feel crook by hour ten.

I'd watch the other blokes heading to the mess for tea. Walking normal. Having a laugh.

Meanwhile I'm hobbling like an old man.

Reckoned maybe I just wasn't cut out for sustained work on concrete. I'm 42. Done construction for 20 years but this was my first FIFO gig. Maybe my body couldn't cop the intensity.

But it didn't make sense. First swing felt sweet. Second swing started getting rough. By my 3rd swing I was cooked.

Started trying to sort it out.

Changed boots first. $290 on different steel caps. Bloke in the crib room reckoned they were the goods. Felt amazing for about a week. Then right back to that bone-grinding feeling.

Bought some Oliver boots instead on my RnR. $315. Composite toes. Lighter weight. Thought that'd do the trick.

Same thing. First few days of my 4th swing felt better. By day six, feet were on fire again.

Tried gel insoles from the chemist on my break. $60. The thick ones with heaps of reviews. L…

data.caption: It's not anxiety. It's your arteries.
data.copy:
The more you think about whether it'll work tonight—the more likely it won't.

You know exactly what I'm talking about.

She touches your leg at dinner. Or leans in close on the couch. Or gives you that look you used to love.

And instead of feeling excited, you feel dread.

Because the second you realize where this is heading, your brain starts running.

"Will it work this time?"

"What if it doesn't?"

"What if I can't get hard?"

"What if I lose it halfway through again?"

And once those thoughts start, you can't shut them off.

You're trying to be present. Trying to focus on her. Trying to enjoy the moment. But you're not really there anymore.

You're in your head. Monitoring. Checking. Watching yourself from the outside like you're taking an exam you know you're going to fail.

Is it working yet? How hard am I? Is this hard enough? Can I maintain this?

And the more you think about it, the more anxious you get.

And the more anxious you get, the more likely it is to fail.

It's like trying to fall asleep by thinking "I need to fall asleep right now." The harder you try, the more impossible it becomes.

Everyone tells you the same useless advice.

"Just relax."

"Stop thinking about it."

"Get out of your head."

Like you haven't tried that a thousand times already.

Like you can just turn off the part of your brain that's terrified of failing again.

But here's what nobody's telling you—and this is the part that changes everything.

That anxiety isn't the problem. It's a symptom.

You're not broken. You're not weak. You don't have a mental problem.

You have a circulation problem that created the anxiety in the first place.

Let me explain how this actually works.

The first time it happened, it probably came out of nowhere. You were fine. Everything was normal. Then suddenly, mid-session, you started losing it.

Maybe you'd had a few drinks. Maybe you were stressed from work. Maybe you were just tired.

Whatever the reason, it happened once.

data.caption: 9 weeks between appointments. After 7 years of going every 5.
data.copy:
My colorist said something last Tuesday that made me put down my phone.

"You could've waited a few more weeks, honestly."

She'd been doing my roots every five weeks for seven years. Same chair. Same small talk. Same $220 plus tip. And now she was standing behind me, running her fingers through my part, looking genuinely surprised.

"Your regrowth is way less than usual. What changed?"

Let me back up.

I'm 43. I run a marketing agency. I manage a team of eleven people, two kids under ten, and a husband who thinks "meal prep" means ordering Uber Eats on Sunday.

I do not have time for things that don't work. If something earns a spot in my routine, it's because it performs.

But hair coloring? That wasn't a routine. That was a hostage situation.

Every five weeks, like clockwork, I'd see them. Those wiry little traitors at my temples. Bright white against dark brown. By week four, they weren't subtle anymore. They were announcing themselves. And by week five, I couldn't leave the house without checking every mirror and every car window reflection to see if my part was giving me away.

So I'd book the appointment. Cancel something on my calendar. Drive 25 minutes. Sit for two and a half hours. Pay $220. Drive home.

And then I'd do the math that every woman who colors has done quietly in her head:

$220 every five weeks. That's $2,288 a year. Almost $23,000 over a decade.

Twenty-three thousand dollars. Not to fix anything. Just to keep up.

But the money wasn't even the worst part. The worst part was that tiny window — three, maybe four good weeks — before the roots started creeping back in and the whole cycle reset.

I think what finally broke me wasn't vanity. It was exhaustion. I was tired of being on the treadmill of a fight I couldn't win, only maintain.

I mentioned this to a friend at school pickup. Just a throwaway line: "I can't believe I'm spending this much to cover my roots every month."

She looked at me for a second. "I used to go every five weeks…

data.caption: upairy.com
data.copy:
My 4-year-old is still in diapers.

And I genuinely don't understand why.

My name is Bec I'm 31 years old.

And for two years, I've been trying to figure out why my daughter won't potty train.

Not "won't try."

Won't train.

She's smart. She can read some words. She knows her numbers. 

She follows instructions perfectly.

But potty training? Nothing sticks.

And the confusing part is her younger brother trained at 2 and a half.

No issues. No drama. He just got it.

So what's different?

We first tried when she was 2 and a half.

I read the books. Did the 3-day method. Set aside a long weekend.

Day one was rough. Lots of accidents. But I expected that.

Day two, she seemed to be getting it.

Day three, complete shutdown.

Refused the potty. Held her pee for five hours. Had a meltdown.

I figured okay, she's not ready yet. We'll try again in a few months.

We tried again at 3.

Same pattern. A few days of progress, then total resistance.

Back to diapers.

Tried again at 3 and a half. Same thing.

Every time, it was like hitting a wall.

She'd make a little progress. Then something would shut down. She'd refuse. We'd stop.

I talked to her pediatrician.

She said some kids are more resistant. 

To keep trying.

Stay consistent.

I talked to other moms.

They said maybe she's stubborn. Maybe she needs different rewards. Maybe she has a fear.

I tried everything they suggested.

Different rewards. Special potty seats. Songs. Books. Stickers. Screen time.

Nothing worked.

And then her little brother started showing interest.

He was 2 and a half. Watching her sit on the potty sometimes.

One day he asked to try.

He went. Just like that.

Two weeks later, he was trained.

No meltdowns. No resistance. He just figured it out.

And my daughter? Still in diapers.

I kept thinking there had to be a reason.

She wasn't being stubborn for no reason.

Kids don't refuse to learn something for two years just because.

There had to be something I was missing.

keyword.description: Free-text search string (lowercased server-side). Use for product names, brands, hooks, domains — not for category/niche (use niches).
keyword.allowed_values: Any string; empty = no text filter.

searchkeyword.description: Which ad field keyword searches. NOT a niche/category selector.
searchkeyword.allowed_values: All, landingurl, pagename, adtext, productname. Default All when keyword is set.

countries.description: Ad target countries (where the ad runs — wlads.countries). Not store HQ.
countries.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.
countries.notes: MX/CO/CL are not in this Meta targeting catalog. Use store_based_in for stores based in those markets.

excludeCountries.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.

storebasedin.description: Store Based In (dashboard storebasedin → store_traffic.shop_origin_country). Use for Mexico/Colombia/Chile/etc. store HQ.
storebasedin.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2 including MX, CO, CL, AR, PE and other Explore Shops Based In markets.

niches.description: Product category / vertical filter (dashboard Meta niches). Use when user asks for a category, niche, vertical, or market — not keyword.
niches.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: CG, AM, GG, JY, GS, HT, BY, BG, SK, WC, MC, SP, KS, TS, HE, PS, DP, HI, FT, OG, OP, TR, AC, AA, BM, FK, SH, SW, EL, FW, WT, EW, FR, GM, PH, EC, WE, SC, BE, MU, PA, CB, CF, CP, DC, CT, HH, SG, YG, CC, PZ, LS, GP, WN, SF, OR, MG, PB. See allowed_niches in response for code→label map. Fashion/clothing = CG.

website.description: Detected store/checkout technology on the landing page (dashboard Website filter).
website.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: SH, TP, BU, LS, CC, SL, TA, GG, FU, CS, LP, FO, SI, GP, XS, YC, HY, DI, MS, SB, PP, WC, TT, TW, PI, GO, SC, FB, MG, WP, SQ, PS, GM, KV, CO, HJ, WX, AR, BC, MC. SH=Shopify, WC=WooCommerce, CS=Clickfunnels. See allowed_technologies in response.

languages.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

excludeLanguages.allowed_values: Comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

apps.description: Shopify apps detected on the store.
apps.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated app names/ids from dashboard Apps filter. See allowed_apps in response.

excludeApps.description: Exclude stores using these Shopify apps.
excludeApps.allowed_values: Comma-separated app names/ids. See allowed_apps in response.

themes.description: Shopify theme name on the store (exact match).
themes.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated exact theme names from dashboard Themes filter (discover via GET /api/themes).

scaling.allowed_values: rising, stable, declining, nodownscaling, upscaling, downscaling.

mediafilter.allowed_values: videos, images, carousel, dco. Omit/All = all formats.

pagetypefilter.allowed_values: products, collections, funnels, nofunnels. Empty/All = all types.

adscorefilter.description: WinningHunter ad score tier (Established / Has Potential / Unestablished).
adscorefilter.allowed_values: winning (Established), scaling (Has Potential), testing (Unestablished). Requires matching account tier.

lowimpressions.description: Hide ads with very low impressions.
lowimpressions.allowed_values: hide (exclude low-impression rows). Omit = show all.

rankgrowthfilter.description: Within-brand ad rank momentum vs historic rank_history.
rankgrowthfilter.allowed_values: Comma-separated subset of: rising, stable, declining.

minadrank.description: Minimum within-brand ad rank (lower rank number = stronger ad for that brand, e.g. #1).

min.description: Minimum duplicate/active-seen ad count on the page.

minactiveads.description: Minimum active Meta ads on the advertiser Facebook page (total_active_ads_on_page).
minactiveads.notes: find_winning_products auto-applies minactiveads=50 for US when not set (see forced block).

minactiveadsgrowth.description: Minimum page active-ads percent growth over activeadsgrowthperiod.
minactiveadsgrowth.allowed_values: Human percent (25 = 25%); negatives allowed for decline.

activeadsgrowthperiod.description: Lookback window for active-ads growth filter.
activeadsgrowthperiod.allowed_values: 1w, 1m, 3m. Default 1m when min/max growth set. 1w=1 week, 1m=1 month, 3m=3 months.
activeadsgrowthperiod.notes: 14d/2m exist on the dashboard but are omitted from MCP — sparse wlads baselines return empty result sets.

minpagelikes.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. Ads missing the field excluded when min set.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.
